content: Thy-1, also known as CD90, is a highly conserved cell surface protein with a molecular weight of 25–37 kDa. It is heavily N-glycosylated and anchored to the cell membrane via a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) linkage. Structurally, it contains a single V-like immunoglobulin domain and was initially identified as an antigen on thymocytes. Thy-1 serves as a marker for various stem cells and is also expressed in the axonal processes of mature neurons. Its structural study contributed to the foundation of the immunoglobulin superfamily, of which it is the smallest member. Additionally, Thy-1 was pivotal in the early biochemical characterization of vertebrate GPI anchors and demonstrated tissue-specific differential glycosylation for the first time. Thy-1 was the first T-cell marker to be identified. It was discovered in 1964 by Reif and Allen during their search for heterologous antisera against mouse leukemia cells. They found it to be present on murine thymocytes, T lymphocytes, and neuronal cells. Initially named the theta (θ) antigen, it was later renamed Thy-1 (Thymocyte differentiation antigen 1) due to its identification in thymocytes, which are precursors of T cells in the thymus. The human homolog of Thy-1 was isolated in 1980 as a 25 kDa protein (p25) from the T-lymphoblastoid cell line MOLT-3. The discovery of Thy-1 in both mice and humans led to the identification of many other T-cell markers, which are critical to the field of immunology, as T cells are major components of the adaptive immune response. The Thy-1 gene is highly conserved across vertebrate evolution and is even found in some invertebrates. Homologs have been described in species such as squid, frogs, chickens, mice, rats, dogs, and humans. In humans, the Thy-1 gene is located on chromosome 11q, close to the CD3 and CD56/NCAM genes. Some researchers speculate that the proximity of these genes may have functional significance, although there is no direct homology. The rodent Thy-1 protein has a 25-kDa core protein composed of 111 or 112 amino acids, with three N-glycosylation sites. In contrast, human Thy-1 has two N-glycosylation sites. The mature Thy-1 protein is transferred to a GPI anchor after the removal of a C-terminal transmembrane domain present in its precursor form. Thy-1 is one of the most heavily glycosylated membrane proteins, with carbohydrates accounting for up to 30% of its molecular mass. In most species, it has three N-glycosylation sites but no O-glycosylation. The glycosylation patterns of Thy-1 vary between tissues, with brain Thy-1 containing galactosamine and thymic Thy-1 having an excess of sialic acid. This tissue-specific glycosylation was first demonstrated in Thy-1, making it a historic example of cell type-specific glycosylation on an invariant protein. Thy-1 expression varies between species and cell types. It is expressed on thymocytes, neurons, mesenchymal stem cells, hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), natural killer (NK) cells, endothelial cells, renal glomerular mesangial cells, circulating metastatic melanoma cells, follicular dendritic cells, and a subset of fibroblasts and myofibroblasts. In mice, Thy-1 is found on thymocytes, peripheral T cells, myoblasts, epidermal cells, and keratinocytes. It is considered a pan T-cell marker in mice, similar to CD2, CD5, and CD28. In humans, Thy-1 is expressed on endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, a subset of CD34+ bone marrow cells, umbilical cord blood cells, cardiac fibroblasts, and fetal liver-derived hematopoietic cells. In the nervous system, Thy-1 expression is predominantly neuronal, although some glial cells also express it during later stages of differentiation. Thy-1 levels in the brain are developmentally regulated, increasing significantly during postnatal development as the brain matures. Thy-1 expression in lymphoid tissue is highly variable between species. In humans, it is restricted to a small population of cortical thymocytes and is not expressed in mature T cells. In mice, it is the most abundant glycoprotein on thymocytes, with approximately one million copies per cell. Mouse cortical thymocytes express higher levels of Thy-1 than medullary thymocytes, which in turn express more than lymph node cells. In rats, Thy-1 is only expressed on thymocytes and is lost at an earlier stage of T-cell maturation compared to mice. Thy-1 expression can be induced by various agents, including thymopoietin, thymosin, prostaglandins, nerve growth factor, interleukin-1 (IL-1), tumor necrosis factor (TNF), phorbol myristate acetate (PMA), calcium ionophores, and diacylglycerol (DAG). As a GPI-anchored protein, Thy-1 is localized to the outer leaflet of lipid rafts in the cell membrane. In neurons, it is strongly expressed in mature axons but is absent from axons during growth and temporarily suppressed during axonal injury. Thy-1 interacts with inhibitory G proteins, the Src family kinase c-fyn, and tubulin within lipid rafts. It is also incorporated into HIV-1 virus particles during viral budding from cells. The precise function of Thy-1 remains incompletely understood. It is thought to play roles in cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions, with implications in neurite outgrowth, nerve regeneration, apoptosis, metastasis, inflammation, and fibrosis. Thy-1 knockout mice are viable and appear grossly normal but exhibit deficits in social learning and cognition, which can be rescued by transgenic Thy-1 expression or pharmacological treatment with GABA(A) receptor antagonists. This suggests that Thy-1 knockout mice have excessive GABAergic inhibition in the dentate gyrus and impaired long-term potentiation. Thy-1 is involved in axon growth regulation. Crosslinking anti-Thy-1 antibodies can promote neurite outgrowth, which depends on Gαi and the activation of Land N-type calcium channels. Thy-1 interacts with beta-3 integrins, and its interaction with beta-3 integrins on mature astrocytes may halt axon growth. In T cells, crosslinking Thy-1 molecules in lipid rafts can substitute for T-cell receptor (TCR) signaling or CD28 costimulation, depending on the context. Thy-1 aggregation induced by crosslinking antibodies causes apoptosis in thymocytes and mesangial cells, despite upregulation of the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2. In mesangial cells, this cell death appears to be apoptosis based on TUNEL and annexin V staining, but electron microscopy suggests necrosis. Anti-Thy-1 antibodies are used in nephrology to induce experimental mesangioproliferative glomerulonephritis in rats, a model known as anti-Thy-1 GN. Thy-1 has also been shown to act as a tumor suppressor in certain cancers, potentially through upregulation of thrombospondin, SPARC (osteonectin), and fibronectin. However, it may also facilitate extravasation in circulating melanoma cells. In prostate cancer, Thy-1 is expressed in cancer-associated stroma but not in normal stroma, suggesting its potential as a target for cancer-specific drug therapies. Thy-1 mediates cell adhesion, extravasation, and migration through interactions with integrins and possibly other receptors. It facilitates the adhesion of leukocytes and monocytes to endothelial cells and fibroblasts, melanoma cells to endothelium, and thymocytes to thymic epithelium. Thy-1 expression is upregulated in activated endothelial cells and interacts with the leukocyte integrin Mac-1 (CD11b/CD18), potentially playing a role in leukocyte homing and recruitment. In fibrosis, Thy-1 expression varies by tissue. In lung fibrosis, Thy-1 levels are suppressed in activated fibroblasts, and Thy-1 knockout mice exhibit increased lung fibrosis. These mice also show heightened fibrosis in response to radiation or bleomycin, a chemotherapeutic agent. Thy-1 knockout mice display impaired cutaneous immune responses and abnormal retinal development, including thinning of several retinal layers. Thy-1 is a major marker of hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) pluripotency, often used in combination with CD34 for fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS). It is also a marker for other stem cell types, such as mesenchymal stem cells, hepatic stem cells, keratinocyte stem cells, and putative endometrial progenitor/stem cells.
